On 20 November 2026, Levent Alpöge posted a [short remark](https://alpo.ge/remark.pdf) and a
1.4 GB [Lean 4 project](https://alpo.ge/lean.tar.gz.part01) claiming a machine-checked proof of the
Riemann Hypothesis, along with the Riemann Hypothesis for every Dirichlet L-function. Lean is a proof
assistant: if its kernel accepts a proof, every step has been checked mechanically. That turns
"is this proof right?" into a question anyone with a computer can answer, if they are careful about
what exactly they check.

Within hours, people in the Lean community had built and checked it (see the
[forum thread](https://leanprover.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/113488-general/topic/Discussion.3A.20Alp.C3.B6ge.20Proves.20the.20Riemann.20Hypothesis)).
The most complete public record is [Andrew Sutherland's page](https://math.mit.edu/~drew/grh/). I wanted
to do it myself, end to end, for my own understanding. This page is that run. It updates as each step
finishes, and every result on it is quoted from the run's logs.

## What a check can and can't tell you

A passing check means the Lean kernel, and several independent checkers, accepted a proof of five exact
formal statements from Lean's three standard axioms. It does **not** mean:

- that anyone understands the proof. It is 175,187 files and about 17 million lines, written with AI;
- that the formal statements mean what we think. That is why they are printed below, and why the main one
  is Mathlib's own definition, written long before this project existed;
- that every checker can't share one bug. Using checkers written independently, in different languages,
  some with formal proofs of their own soundness, makes that very unlikely.

## The five statements

The proof is judged against these statements, which import nothing but Mathlib. Each is proved with
`sorry`, Lean's placeholder for "not proved here"; the project has to supply the real proofs under the same
names. I wrote this file independently. Apart from comments it is identical to the community's
[`Challenge.lean`](https://github.com/Deicyde/riemann-hypothesis/blob/main/src/Challenge.lean), and built
with my Mathlib their file exports to exactly the same bytes they published.

```lean
import Mathlib

def RiemannZetaZerosOnLine : Prop :=
  ∀ s : ℂ, riemannZeta s = 0 → (¬∃ n : ℕ, s = -2 * ((n : ℂ) + 1)) → s ≠ 1 → s.re = 1 / 2

def DirichletLNonvanishingRightOfHalf : Prop :=
  ∀ (N : ℕ) [NeZero N] (χ : DirichletCharacter ℂ N) (s : ℂ),
    1 / 2 < s.re → (χ ≠ 1 ∨ s ≠ 1) → DirichletCharacter.LFunction χ s ≠ 0

def DirichletLZerosOnLine : Prop :=
  ∀ (N : ℕ) [NeZero N] (χ : DirichletCharacter ℂ N) (s : ℂ),
    0 < s.re → s.re < 1 → DirichletCharacter.LFunction χ s = 0 → s.re = 1 / 2

def PrimitiveDirichletLZerosOnLine : Prop :=
  ∀ (N : ℕ) [NeZero N] (χ : DirichletCharacter ℂ N), χ.IsPrimitive →
    ∀ s : ℂ, 0 < s.re → s.re < 1 → DirichletCharacter.LFunction χ s = 0 → s.re = 1 / 2

theorem riemannHypothesis : RiemannHypothesis := by sorry
theorem riemannZeta_eq_zero_re : RiemannZetaZerosOnLine := by sorry
theorem LFunction_ne_zero_of_half_lt_re : DirichletLNonvanishingRightOfHalf := by sorry
theorem LFunction_eq_zero_re : DirichletLZerosOnLine := by sorry
theorem LFunction_eq_zero_re_of_isPrimitive : PrimitiveDirichletLZerosOnLine := by sorry
```

| Theorem | In words |
|---|---|
| `riemannHypothesis` | Mathlib's `RiemannHypothesis`: every zero of ζ other than −2, −4, −6, … (and the pole at 1) has real part ½. |
| `riemannZeta_eq_zero_re` | The same statement, written out. |
| `LFunction_ne_zero_of_half_lt_re` | For every modulus N and Dirichlet character χ, L(χ, s) ≠ 0 when Re s > ½, except at the pole χ = 1, s = 1. |
| `LFunction_eq_zero_re` | Every zero of every Dirichlet L-function in the strip 0 < Re s < 1 has Re s = ½. |
| `LFunction_eq_zero_re_of_isPrimitive` | The same, for primitive characters. |

I'm not a number theorist, so I don't rely on my own reading of the last four. They have to match the
project's definitions term for term, which the checkers enforce, and they agree with the version reviewed
in public by people who are.

## How the check works

I treated the project as untrusted code. Building a Lean project runs code it contains (tactics, macros,
build commands), so nothing from it ran on my own machine, and nothing that loads it ran outside a sandbox.

1. **A fresh virtual machine** with its own kernel. Every tool is pinned to an exact commit and verified,
   and the project is downloaded and checked inside the VM.
2. **No network** once the downloads are done. Mathlib, the math library the project builds on, is then
   compiled from source and compared file by file with Mathlib's official build cache.
3. **The statements first.** The challenge file is built and exported before any project code runs.
4. **A sandbox for the project.** The build runs under [Landlock](https://landlock.io) via
   [landrun](https://github.com/Zouuup/landrun): it can read its sources and the toolchain and write only its
   own build folder. I tested that writes elsewhere, reading SSH keys and network connections all fail before
   starting.
5. **Export, then judge.** The compiled proof is exported to a single file. The judges read only that file, so
   no project code runs while checking. [`lake comparator`](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/)
   checks that the statements match and that only `propext`, `Quot.sound` and `Classical.choice` are used, then
   replays the whole proof through Lean's kernel. Then it goes through every independent checker that fits in
   the VM's memory.

## Checkers

Each checker reads the same exported proof and either accepts it, rejects it, or fails to finish. A
rejection by any one of them would override every acceptance.

{{< include _kernels.md >}}

## Hashes you can compare

A hash pins down exactly which bytes were checked. Matching hashes mean my run checked the same proof as
other public runs, and that the build reproduces bit for bit on a different machine, built a different way
(sandboxed `lake build` here, unsandboxed elsewhere).

{{< include _hashes.md >}}

## Findings along the way

::: {.callout-note title="Mathlib from source matches the official cache, with one exception"}
Of the 8,700 files in Mathlib's official build cache, 8,689 are byte-identical to my from-source build.
Ten belong to the cache tool itself and aren't part of the math. One differs:
`Mathlib/Combinatorics/SimpleGraph/Walk/Operations.olean`, and only in a single auto-generated lemma,
`SimpleGraph.Walk.take.eq_2`. The other 230 constants in that file match. My build of it is deterministic
(rebuilt twice, same bytes), so the cache's copy was produced differently. Both versions are kernel-checked
theorems; this is a reproducibility quirk, not a soundness problem.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="A full build needs about 1.7 TB of bookkeeping"}
For each module, Lake writes a `.setup.json` file listing everything it imports. Here that averages about
7 MB, and a sampled estimate over all 175,187 modules is about 1.7 TB. The files compress about 26× with
zstd, so this run builds on a compressed btrfs disk.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Two problems the tests caught"}
My sandbox wrapper first failed in a way that looked like success: the kernel supports Landlock ABI v6,
landrun asked for v10 and refused to start, and every "access denied" test passed because nothing ran at all.
A positive control (a command that must succeed) now runs first. Separately, the original checker script
counted `sorry` warnings with the wrong quote characters, so that count could never be non-zero; it's
[fixed](https://github.com/kai-do/riemann-hypothesis-lean-check). The axiom check was never affected.
:::

## How I used AI

Claude (Anthropic's AI) set up and ran this check with me: it wrote the scripts, ran the commands and
drafted this page, and I reviewed and directed the work. That is exactly why the check is built so no single
party has to be trusted, including the AI running it. Every result here is read from logs, and the hashes let
anyone confirm the same bytes were checked.
